passage: At the village school ground in the afternoon, Naveen pointed his bat like a king's staff. "Suraj is out. Nobody passes to him," he said, and the others obeyed at once. Naveen liked how quickly they moved. It felt safe to be the one deciding. Suraj sat under the neem tree pulling grass. Then Naveen's kite snagged high on a branch, and he asked two boys to climb. They said their mothers were calling and drifted away. Only Suraj, without being asked, looked up at the kite and said, "I can reach it if you hold my legs." Naveen stood there, red-faced, not sure what to say.

qa.q: Where did Suraj sit while the others played?
qa.a: He sat under the neem tree pulling grass.

qa.q: What might Naveen have been feeling when the two boys drifted away from the kite?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and a little alone, seeing that the boys who obeyed him did not care enough to help.

qa.q: What could Naveen try tomorrow if he wants friends who really stand by him?
qa.a: He could let Suraj back into the game, ask others for their ideas and choose who plays together rather than giving orders.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Naveen stood there red-faced?
qa.a: Suraj may have felt uncertain about whether Naveen would apologise, even though he had chosen to help.

grounding: A group leader enjoys deciding who is in or out, hurts a boy, and discovers that ruling through orders leaves followers who do not care about him.

passage:
"Just say it, Indu," Payal whispered at the lunch benches. "Say Rani smells funny."
"But she doesn't."
"Then you can sit somewhere else."
Indu's hands went cold. She laughed a small laugh that she did not mean, and Rani looked at her food.
"That was not funny," Indu said later, at the tap. "I'm sorry, Rani."
"Why did you do it?"
"I was scared they'd throw me out."
Next day Payal handed her a note to pass around. Indu quietly put it back in Payal's bag and said, "I'm not doing this one." Two girls, Meena and Sonal, shrugged and sat down next to her.

qa.q: Who did Payal want Indu to say smelled funny?
qa.a: Payal wanted Indu to say that Rani smells funny.

qa.q: Why did Indu laugh at first even though she did not mean it?
qa.a: She was scared of being thrown out of the group, so she went along with the mean joke.

qa.q: What small step did Indu take that showed who her real friends were?
qa.a: She refused just one thing, passing the note, and saw that Meena and Sonal still sat down with her.

qa.q: What might Rani have felt when Indu apologised at the tap?
qa.a: Rani may have felt hurt but also a little relieved that Indu admitted she was wrong, though she asked why it happened.

grounding: A child goes along with mean things out of fear of being expelled, then quietly refuses one thing and sees who stands by her.

passage: I am Reena, and last year I used to eat lunch near the popular table just in case someone waved me over. Nobody did. I felt silly all the time. One day I saw Yusuf and Meera at our own class bench, arguing about which bird was on the wall, and they looked happy. So I sat with them. I stopped watching the popular table after a few days. Now we trade stories and stickers, and I learned Meera can imitate every teacher. Being with only two friends is quiet, but I laugh more. Looking back, I did not give up on anything; I just stopped waiting.

qa.q: What were Yusuf and Meera arguing about?
qa.a: They were arguing about which bird was on the wall.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling while sitting near the popular table hoping to be waved over?
qa.a: Reena felt silly and hopeful, wanting to belong but not being noticed.

qa.q: Which change helped Reena, and why did it work?
qa.a: Reena sat with Yusuf and Meera instead of waiting, found friends who liked Reena as they were, and laughed more with them.

qa.q: How might Yusuf and Meera have seen Reena joining them?
qa.a: They probably welcomed Reena, since they went on sharing stories and stickers and included Reena easily.

grounding: A child stops chasing the popular group and enjoys their two friends; a smaller circle feels deeper.

passage:
Monday: Sumita walked past Mridul at the school gate without waiting. She was talking with the group from Class 5B and did not look back. Mridul felt heat behind his eyes.
Wednesday: Mridul told his older cousin that he was angry and that his stomach hurt. The cousin listened and did not say much. Mridul had thought of hiding Sumita's pencil box, but he let that thought go by.
Following Tuesday: Sumita came up at recess and mumbled, "I miss playing marbles with you." Her shoulders were tight. Mridul said, "I'm still upset. But you can sit here today." Sumita sat. She looked as if she was torn between two places.

qa.q: Which group was Sumita talking with at the school gate?
qa.a: She was talking with the group from Class 5B.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling on Monday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry; there was heat behind his eyes when Sumita walked past.

qa.q: What did Mridul do with his anger that kept it from turning into revenge?
qa.a: He told his older cousin how he felt and let go of the idea of hiding Sumita's pencil box.

qa.q: What might Sumita have been feeling when she came to Mridul at recess?
qa.a: Sumita probably felt torn and guilty, wanting her old friend but not wanting to lose the new group, which her tight shoulders and mumble suggest.

grounding: A child is dropped by a friend who joined the clique, feels betrayed and angry, tells someone, avoids revenge and leaves the door open.

passage:
"Sir, you want me to hold the register?" Jahnavi asked, hovering by the staff-room door.
"Thank you, Jahnavi." Rafiq Sir rubbed his eyes.
"You look tired today."
"A little. My mother is unwell, and I slept badly. Nothing you need to worry about."
Jahnavi nodded. In class she did not fidget or talk, and when the chalk box fell she picked up the pieces before anyone laughed. At the bell she stacked the notebooks neatly on his desk.
"Jahnavi," he said, "that helped more than you know."
She smiled. "I hope your mother feels better, Sir."

qa.q: What did Rafiq Sir say was wrong when Jahnavi told him he looked tired?
qa.a: He said his mother was unwell and he had slept badly.

qa.q: What made Jahnavi behave calmly and kindly in class that day?
qa.a: She noticed her teacher looked tired and worried and understood he was a person with troubles, so she chose to be quiet and helpful.

qa.q: What else could Jahnavi do on a day her teacher looks stressed?
qa.a: She could help carry books, keep her voice low and be patient, without prying into what is wrong.

qa.q: How might Rafiq Sir have felt when Jahnavi stacked the notebooks?
qa.a: He probably felt touched and a little less alone, which is why he said her help mattered more than she knew. 🙂

grounding: A child notices a tired, worried teacher, sees him as a person and offers small helpful acts.

passage: Prize-day rehearsal was in ten minutes, and the hall was full of drums and chairs scraping. Parul Ma'am snapped, "Vasudha, stop talking! You are ruining this," though it was the boy behind her who had been talking. Vasudha's ears burned. She had always thought Parul Ma'am was the fairest teacher. She said nothing through the whole practice. Afterwards, when the hall emptied, Vasudha walked up and said, "Ma'am, I felt bad when you said it was me. It was not." Parul Ma'am paused, then said, "I was rushed and I got it wrong. I am sorry."

qa.q: How much time was left before the prize-day rehearsal in the passage?
qa.a: There were ten minutes left before the rehearsal.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when Parul Ma'am blamed her?
qa.a: She was shocked and hurt, since her ears burned and she had thought Parul Ma'am was the fairest teacher.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do well by waiting until the hall emptied?
qa.a: She spoke politely and privately about how she felt, which gave the teacher a chance to admit the mistake without being embarrassed. 🙂

qa.q: How might Parul Ma'am have seen the situation while rushing?
qa.a: She was under time pressure in a noisy hall and probably reacted without looking carefully, then recognised her error when Vasudha spoke up.

grounding: A child is shocked when her favourite teacher is unfair, then politely tells her how she felt without cutting her off.

passage: I sit behind Nikita in maths, so I notice things. Every time Mrs. Rao passes our row, she stops at Dev's and Anya's desks and says, "Lovely work." Nikita's hand goes up for questions and sometimes gets skipped. Yesterday she wrote a long answer and looked around after, but the teacher did not check her page. Nikita put her head down for a bit. I don't know whether the teacher meant it or just did not see. Today Nikita went to the front after class and asked for help with a sum, and Mrs. Rao sat down with her. I am Gautam.

qa.q: Which two children does Mrs. Rao praise at their desks?
qa.a: She stops at Dev's and Anya's desks and says, "Lovely work."

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling when she put her head down?
qa.a: She may have felt overlooked and a little sad, though Gautam cannot be sure whether that is what she felt.

qa.q: What could Nikita do if she still feels unseen by her teacher?
qa.a: She can keep doing her best, keep asking for help as she did, and talk to her teacher or a parent if it still seems unfair.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Rao explain her behaviour if asked?
qa.a: She may not have noticed she was giving some children more attention, or she may have simply been busy; it might be real or not.

grounding: A classmate observes a child who feels invisible next to teacher favourites, who asks for help; it may or may not be real favouritism.

passage:
"Jaya, my hands are shaking," Uma whispered in the corridor.
"It's only Ma'am."
"She looks at me and I forget everything, even 5 times 6."
"You could ask her a question after class. Just one small one."
"What if she gets angry?"
"Try."
After the bell, Uma stood at the teacher's desk. "Ma'am, can you tell me again how to do long division?"
The teacher took off her spectacles. "Of course, beti. Sit here." She drew the steps slowly and even smiled. "You should have asked earlier."
Outside, Uma told Jaya, "She is still strict, but she is kind."

qa.q: What did Uma forget when the teacher looked at her?
qa.a: She forgot everything, even 5 times 6.

qa.q: Why was Uma afraid to ask the teacher a question?
qa.a: She feared the teacher would get angry, and her fear of getting things wrong made her hands shake.

qa.q: What small step helped Uma see the teacher differently?
qa.a: She asked one small question after class, when it was quiet, and saw the teacher's softer side.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Uma asked about long division?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt glad that a student came for help, as her smile and "You should have asked earlier" suggest. 😊

grounding: A child scared of a strict teacher asks a question after class and sees her softer side.

passage: The last bus had left, and the small-town school was quiet except for a crow on the roof. Rekha still could not see how three-fourths and six-eighths could be the same. Charu Madam, the fractions teacher, had stayed on after the bell, drawing circles on the slate with a stub of chalk. "Cut this one in four, that one in eight. See?" Rekha counted the pieces, then grinned. "They are equal!" Madam smiled and said, "Take your time." When Rekha's uncle came to walk her home, she said, "Thank you, Madam," and next day was first to finish the homework.

qa.q: What did Charu Madam draw the circles on?
qa.a: She drew circles on the slate with a stub of chalk.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she counted the pieces and grinned?
qa.a: She felt relieved and proud that she finally understood, and she also felt cared for by her teacher who stayed on.

qa.q: What did Rekha do to show her gratitude?
qa.a: She said thank you and worked harder, becoming the first to finish the homework the next day.

qa.q: How might Charu Madam have felt seeing Rekha's grin?
qa.a: She probably felt satisfied and glad that staying late had helped, though she was also tired after school.

grounding: A teacher stays late to help a child understand fractions; the child feels cared for, says thank you and tries harder.

passage: Zubin, come, sit. I am Ritu, your Masi, and I want to tell you about the day I was nine. My teacher read my spelling test aloud, laughed and said, "Is this an elephant's handwriting?" The whole class giggled. I wanted to vanish under the desk. I did not eat that night. When my mother asked, I told her. She did not say I was too sensitive. She said, "You did nothing to deserve that," and the next morning she and my father went to speak to the principal. The teacher never mocked anyone again. I have never forgotten that my mother believed me.

qa.q: What did the teacher say about Ritu's handwriting?
qa.a: The teacher said, "Is this an elephant's handwriting?"

qa.q: What did nine-year-old Ritu want to do when the class giggled?
qa.a: She wanted to vanish under the desk, which shows how ashamed she felt.

qa.q: What did Ritu's mother do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She listened, said Ritu had done nothing to deserve it and went to the principal with Ritu's father, so Ritu knew she was believed and the school heard about it.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel hearing Masi Ritu's story?
qa.a: Zubin may feel less alone and more willing to tell a parent if a teacher ever shames Zubin.

grounding: An elder recalls being mocked by a teacher, telling her parents and their raising it with the school; adults should correct, not shame.
